One run per configuration and application: run-to-run variation of the AI configurations is unmeasured, and every difference between them is a single observation.

All authors are employees of Snyk, which develops Snyk Code. The Snyk Code product owner is a co-author, and his team shipped a rule update for one of the findings outside the reference set; all main results are reported as run, before that update.

Reference vulnerabilities were partly seeded with OpenAI and Anthropic models, which could favor the AI configurations; some seeding prompts included vulnerable-pattern examples from a Snyk database, and five applications had been used in Snyk demonstrations, which could favor Snyk Code. The net effect is unknown.
Without the five demonstration applications, Snyk Code matches 74 and Opus 5 xhigh 72 of the remaining 87 vulnerabilities, and they remain the top two.

The reference set can omit real vulnerabilities; measured precision is a lower bound. One known defect makes one vulnerability unmatchable; correcting it raises Claude Code /security-review with Opus 5 medium + Snyk MCP from 80 to 81 and Opus 5 xhigh from 85 to 86, and the union of all seven to 102.
The two-line tolerance, the endpoint rule and one-to-one credit are choices, not facts about the tools; the robustness section shows which conclusions depend on them.
Snyk Code is the only SAST engine evaluated; statements about deterministic SAST are measured on Snyk Code and may not hold for other engines.
Results belong to the configurations as run, including versions and modes; the design cannot separate harness from model.
Cost, token and time figures come from single runs; unavailable costs are excluded, never treated as zero.
Class names follow Snyk Code's vocabulary; findings labeled outside it could go uncredited. The measured effect is small: removing the reference set's alternative class names changes one match.
The origin of each vulnerability, and which model seeded which application, were not recorded.

The archive does not record the Snyk CLI version (the operator reported it after the run), and the Snyk MCP server ran unpinned, so its version is inferred; exact re-execution of those rows is bounded, re-scoring is not.

Codex Security ran in its standard full-repository mode, not its deep mode, and its scans reported partial coverage on 7, 6 and 3 of the 20 applications for GPT-5.6 Luna, Terra and Sol; partial scans are scored as returned.
Five failed attempts preceded the scored success in 4 of the 180 runs; only the final attempt is scored.
Several applications are intentionally vulnerable demonstrations, many vulnerabilities were seeded, and Java is thin; how the results carry over to production code bases is untested.
